subject: English
name: English, Year 8
syllabus: Victorian Curriculum F-10 Version 2.0: English, Level 8

points.title: Language and relationships
points.brief: How formal or casual we are, the names we call people and how we ask for things shape relationships and show roles, such as student and teacher.

points.title: Modality
points.brief: Words such as might, should and must show how certain or forceful a writer is, from low to high modality.

points.title: Figurative language in judgements
points.brief: A simile or metaphor can pack an opinion into an image, such as calling a decision a slap in the face, adding a judgement as well as a picture.

points.title: Hybrid texts
points.brief: A hybrid text mixes the structures and features of more than one text type, such as a story told through diary entries and news reports.

points.title: Building an analytical paragraph
points.brief: A strong paragraph makes a claim, supports it with evidence, explains how the evidence proves the claim, and links back to the main argument.

points.title: Embedding quotations
points.brief: Short quotations work best woven into your own sentence so it still reads smoothly, rather than dropped in on their own.

points.title: Main and subordinate clauses
points.brief: A main clause makes sense on its own. A subordinate clause adds information but depends on the main clause to make sense.

points.title: Embedded clauses
points.brief: An embedded clause sits inside another clause to add detail about a noun, often starting with who, which or that.

points.title: Nominalisation
points.brief: Turning a verb or adjective into a noun, such as decide into decision, makes writing sound more formal and less personal.

points.title: Semicolons
points.brief: A semicolon joins two closely linked main clauses without a joining word, and separates list items that already contain commas.

points.title: Dashes for emphasis and asides
points.brief: A dash can set off an aside or add a sudden twist at the end of a sentence, and is less formal than brackets or a colon.

points.title: Academic vocabulary
points.brief: Words used for study across subjects, such as analyse, significant, consequently and evidence, which make writing precise and formal.

points.title: Connotation
points.brief: Words with the same basic meaning can carry different feelings, such as slim and skinny, and writers choose between them on purpose.

points.title: Intertextuality in images and film
points.brief: A poster, advertisement or film scene can echo a famous painting, film or story, and the reference adds a layer of meaning for viewers who notice it.

points.title: Values in literary texts
points.brief: Characters' choices and how the story treats them show the values of individuals and groups, such as loyalty, fairness or ambition.

points.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander perspectives in literature
points.brief: Texts by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander authors can share perspectives on identity, community and history that readers should consider in the author's own context.

points.title: A writer's style
points.brief: Style is the way a writer writes, built from their word choice, sentence patterns, devices and structure, and readers form opinions about it.

points.title: Positioning readers on ethical issues
points.brief: Writers lead readers to approve or disapprove of a character or choice through what they show, what they leave out and how they describe it.

points.title: Intertextual references in literature
points.brief: A reference to a myth, fairy tale or well-known story lets a writer borrow its meaning, and recognising it gives the reader a new understanding.

points.title: Tone
points.brief: Tone is the writer's attitude that comes through the words, such as playful, bitter or serious.

points.title: Narrative voice
points.brief: Voice is the personality of the narrator that readers hear in the writing, made by word choice, sentence rhythm and attitude.

points.title: Sentence patterns for effect
points.brief: Short sentences can build tension or shock, long flowing ones can slow the pace, and repeated patterns can build emphasis.

points.title: Imagery
points.brief: Imagery is description that appeals to the senses, creating pictures, sounds and feelings in the reader's mind.

points.title: Genre conventions
points.brief: Each genre has familiar features readers expect, such as a mystery's clues and suspects or a fantasy's invented world and magic.

points.title: Foreshadowing
points.brief: Foreshadowing drops hints about what will happen later, building suspense and making the ending feel earned.

points.title: Flashback
points.brief: A flashback interrupts the story to show an earlier event, revealing a character's past or explaining the present.

points.title: Stated and implied meaning
points.brief: A text's stated meaning is what it says outright, its implied meaning is what it suggests, and discussions can support or challenge either.

points.title: Register in speaking
points.brief: Register is how formal our language is. A speech to a school assembly needs a different register from a chat with friends.

points.title: Representation of people, places and events
points.brief: Texts show a version of people, places and events, not the whole truth, and that version reflects when, where and by whom the text was made.

points.title: Word families for spelling
points.brief: Linking a word to its family, such as sign, signal and signature, shows letters you cannot hear and helps you spell it.

points.title: Homophones
points.brief: Homophones sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning, such as their, there and they're, or affect and effect.

points.title: Common endings in academic words
points.brief: Choosing between endings that sound alike, such as -tion and -sion, -ance and -ence, or -able and -ible, in subject words.

points.title: Perspective and bias
points.brief: A perspective is the viewpoint a text comes from. Bias is when a text favours one side, by its word choice or by what it leaves out.

points.title: How quotations can be repurposed
points.brief: A quotation taken out of its context can be made to mean something different, so check where it came from and what surrounded it.

points.title: Problem-solution and compare-contrast structures
points.brief: Writers organise ideas by setting out a problem then its solutions, or by comparing and contrasting two things point by point.

points.title: Questioning a text
points.brief: Evaluating a text means asking who made it, why, what evidence it gives and what it leaves out, before accepting its ideas.

points.title: Persuasive techniques
points.brief: Rhetorical questions, inclusive language, emotive words, repetition and expert opinion are common ways to persuade an audience.

points.title: News report structure
points.brief: A news report puts the most important facts first, answering who, what, when, where, why and how, then adds detail in order of importance.

points.title: Revising for clarity and coherence
points.brief: Revising checks that ideas are in a logical order, paragraphs link, and each sentence says exactly what is meant.
